title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome Following Chemotherapy and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Combination in a Patient with Small-Cell Lung Cancer
case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (T1N2M0), hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and diabetes was admitted for his first cycle of carboplatin (AUC 5) and etoposide (100 mg/m2 on days 1–3) with atezolizumab (1200 mg on day 1). The day after treatment, he was found with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 5/15 and a right upper-limb tonic–clonic seizure that became generalized. Despite clonazepam and levetiracetam, focal seizures persisted, prompting transfer to the intensive care unit. On arrival, his blood pressure was 206/108 mmHg, heart and respiratory rates were elevated, and he was afebrile. Neurologically, he had right hemiplegia, right facial paralysis, and a pyramidal syndrome; blood glucose was normal.

Electroencephalography showed left occipital status epilepticus. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced brain CT revealed no evidence of stroke, hemorrhage, or metastases; the Circle of Willis was patent with mild carotid bulb stenosis. Brain MRI on a 3 T scanner demonstrated multiple bilateral subcortical T2-FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the parietal, temporal, occipital, and cerebellar regions—predominantly posterior—with slight right occipital cortical involvement; there was no corresponding diffusion restriction except for a left thalamic ADC restriction. Arterial spin labeling perfusion showed increased perfusion in the left temporo-parieto-occipital region, left thalamus, and right cerebellum; time-of-flight angiography revealed no thrombus. Laboratory studies for autoimmune, infectious, and secondary hypertension etiologies were within normal limits.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of brain metastases — “initial brain CT... showed no evidence of stroke, bleeding or brain metastasis.”  
2. Posterior circulation infarction — “symmetrical posterior distribution, sparing the calcarine and paramedian occipital lobe... were not in favor of any of the differential diagnosis of PRES (posterior circulation infarct...).”  
3. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy — “symmetrical posterior distribution... were not in favor of any of the differential diagnosis of PRES (...progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy...).”  
4. Gliomatosis cerebri — “symmetrical posterior distribution... were not in favor of any of the differential diagnosis of PRES (...gliomatosis cerebri...).”  
5. Severe hypoglycemia — “glycemia was normal.”  
6. Inflammatory cerebral amyloid angiopathy — “symmetrical posterior distribution... were not in favor of any of the differential diagnosis of PRES (...inflammatory cerebral amyloid angiopathy).”  
7. Herpetic encephalopathy — “The clinical context and the absence of fever did not suggest the diagnosis of herpetic encephalopathy.”
